# Alpha scope and known limitations

> **Release status (2026-10-15):** `0.1.0a1` is the version prepared on `main`.
> The `caliber-v0.1.0a1` tag and downloadable release assets have not been
> published. The capabilities below describe the current code and its CI proof;
> use [Alpha install](m-60-alpha-install.md) to build wheels from a checkout until
> the prerelease is available.

CALIBER `0.1.0a1` is an alpha. This page says what it does, what it does not do, and what to
watch for, so you judge it against what it claims. It is the short version of the
[alpha gap analysis](https://github.com/rrahimi-uci/caliber-suite/blob/main/docs/caliber-alpha-gaps.md), which has the evidence and the reasoning.

## What the alpha does

A small team can self-host CALIBER from documented steps ([Alpha install](m-60-alpha-install.md)) and,
through the web app or the Python SDK, do this with an audit trail and honest failure reporting:

1. Author a prompt.
2. Build a test set.
3. Calibrate the prompt to get a candidate with evaluation evidence.
4. Review the candidate and explicitly apply it to the live MLflow alias.
5. See what is live and which job, dataset version and evaluation put it there.
6. Roll it back.

The same loop works for a skill, a tool and a workflow (the extended tier), and, where an object store
is configured, for building and querying a knowledge base.

Two things about the evidence. The language model and the evaluator are real when you give CALIBER an
`OPENAI_API_KEY` (the Docker stack's `auto` setting, in `.env`), and simulated when you do not: calibration
then runs and returns a candidate, but the scores are canned, and every screen, audit row and release record
that carries them says so. `GET /readiness` and `./start.sh` list each AI-backed part as real or simulated
([Real LLM and evaluation](m-60-alpha-install.md#real-llm-and-evaluation)). And the browser journey is proven in CI
on every change, offline, on the simulated defaults; real-model runs are manual (see the release notes).

## Supported setups

| Item | Alpha support |
| --- | --- |
| Database | PostgreSQL. SQLite works for evaluation and demos when MLflow uses its own, separate store. |
| MLflow | A separate `mlflow server` (3.15 or later) over HTTP. Embedded `--app-name caliber` is not supported. |
| Install | Release wheels with a native MLflow, or the Docker Compose stack. |
| Object store | Needed only for knowledge bases and the object-store console. |
| Python | 3.10, 3.11 or 3.12. |

## What is in, preview, and out

| Maturity | Areas |
| --- | --- |
| Core journey | Prompts, test sets, evaluations, calibration, review and Apply, projects and roles, access tokens, audit log, release timeline, readiness |
| Also in the alpha | Skills, tools (trusted authors), workflows, knowledge bases and the object-store console |
| Preview | MCP servers and OpenAPI integrations (off by default; enable with `CALIBER_FEATURE_INTEGRATIONS`), cookbooks (off by default; enable with `CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS`), the Aria assistant and plans (**on** by default; disable with `CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA=false`). The app carries no maturity labels, so the flag state is the only signal |
| Record-only (off by default) | Release-candidate signoff on the Releases page: it records a decision and deploys nothing (off by default; enable with `CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES`) |
| Experimental (off by default) | Workspace releases: release evaluation has no executor in this build (off by default; enable with `CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES`) |
| Not in the alpha | Memory, and the flagged-trace to refinement loop |

The live board, the release timeline and release operations on the Releases page are core and always on. Only
the release-candidate signoff and workspace releases are behind a flag.

## Feature flags

The areas above sit behind four server-side flags. Three are **off by default**; Aria is the exception and
ships **on**. A flag is read once at startup from the process environment, like the other `CALIBER_*`
settings, so restart CALIBER after you change one. A variable you set is on for `true`, `1`, `yes` or `on`
(any case) and off for anything else, even a typo; leaving it unset keeps its shipped default.

| Flag id | Variable | Default | What it turns on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `aria` | `CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA` | **on** | The Aria assistant and plans (preview): the `/assistant/*` and `/aria/*` routes, the Aria panel and the Plans page. Set `CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA=false` for a deployment that wants it off |
| `integrations` | `CALIBER_FEATURE_INTEGRATIONS` | off | MCP servers and OpenAPI integrations (preview): the `/mcp-servers*` and `/openapi-integrations*` routes and their pages. While it is off, a workflow MCP node is reported as unavailable ("A registered MCP server that CALIBER can reach (needs CALIBER_FEATURE_INTEGRATIONS=true)") |
| `cookbooks` | `CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS` | off | Cookbooks (preview): the `/cookbooks*` routes and the Cookbooks page |
| `release_candidates` | `CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES` | off | Release-candidate signoff and workspace releases (record-only and experimental): the `/releases/candidates*`, `/releases/report-jobs*` and `/projects/{id}/releases*` routes and the candidate part of the Releases page |

For example, Aria is already on; to also try the cookbooks:

```bash
export CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS=true
```

Things to know before you turn one on:

- **Turning a flag on means you accept the behavior of that area.** Preview areas may change or be removed
  without notice. A release-candidate signoff records a decision and deploys or rolls back nothing, and a
  workspace release evaluation stays queued because nothing in this build executes it. Enabling a flag does
  not move an area into the supported journey.
- **The areas depend on each other.** The twenty cookbooks build on other areas, so a lab can need more than
  `CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS`: labs 12 to 15 need `CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA`, labs 05 and 19 need
  `CALIBER_FEATURE_INTEGRATIONS`, and labs 11 and 21 need `CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES`. Each lab's
  README names the flags it needs.
- **Aria also backs a few helpers inside supported pages.** The **Ask Aria** button, **Describe it** prompt
  drafting, the prompt Playground, test-case generation and test runs inside the prompt workspace, and the tool
  unit-test generator call the assistant; these are visible out of the box since Aria ships on, but if you set
  `CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA=false` they are hidden or show a notice that names the variable (the Playground stage
  stays listed and says so). Aria ships on but needs an engine key (`OPENAI_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) to
  answer: until one is set, the **Ask Aria** button is disabled with the reason, the Aria panel opens with the
  reason at the top, and **Describe it** fails with the same message instead of drafting anything. The core journey does not need them: build the test set by hand on the Test Sets
  page, or load it with **Import from file** (JSON Lines or a JSON array).
- **A disabled area answers 404.** Every route of a disabled area returns HTTP 404 with the machine-readable
  `reason_code` `feature_disabled`, so a client can tell "this deployment has it off" from "no such record"
  (the body is shown below).
- **Feature detection.** `GET /capabilities` returns a `features` object keyed by the four ids, each with
  `enabled`, `env_var`, `label` and `stability`, so a client reads the flags without provoking a 404. The web
  app does the same: it hides the navigation entries of a disabled area and shows a "This isn't available on this
  deployment" panel naming the variable if you open one of its URLs directly.
- **The Docker stack passes the variables through.** They carry the same defaults there (Aria on, the other
  three off); set them in the suite-root `.env` (see `.env.example`). See
  [Alpha install](m-60-alpha-install.md#enabling-preview-areas).

A call to a route of a disabled area looks like this:

```json
{
  "detail": "Cookbooks is disabled in this deployment. Set CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS=true to enable it.",
  "status_code": 404,
  "reason_code": "feature_disabled"
}
```

## Known limitations

These are real and deliberate for the alpha. Read them before you rely on the product.

- **No trace-to-refinement automation.** Nothing watches MLflow for flagged traces. There is no feedback
  poller and no "flag this trace" action in the app, and verifying an item in the queue does not start a
  job. Calibration starts from a prompt and a test set, which you create. Submitting feedback on a trace
  records an assessment in MLflow and an audit row, and does nothing else.
- **Traces are scoped by experiment ownership in CALIBER, not in MLflow.** The observability pages, the
  trace, metric and feedback routes, and the Gateway usage tab show a non-admin only the traces filed
  under an MLflow experiment that an agent or workflow they can see is bound to (an agent's
  `experiment_id`, a workflow's `default_experiment_id`); the same rule gates adding a trace to an
  evaluation dataset or a review queue. A trace in any other experiment is hidden from non-admins,
  including workflow runs recorded under a named experiment when the workflow sets no
  `default_experiment_id`. An admin sees every trace, as an admin sees every agent, workflow and run.
  An experiment cannot be claimed by a different project or user once it is bound, **under any alias**:
  a claim is compared on the experiment id the tracking backend assigns, so naming project B's experiment
  by its numeric id, its name or a second name of the same experiment is refused (409), and a claim whose
  experiment cannot be resolved is refused with 503, never guessed. An experiment that two projects
  already claim from before this check is hidden from everyone but an admin until an operator removes
  one of the claims (`GET /observability/experiment-claim-conflicts`, admin only). One that nobody has
  bound yet goes to whoever binds it first; proving ownership needs CALIBER to create the experiment,
  which is planned work. **MLflow's own UI and API run on the same server and are not
  scoped**: anyone who can reach the MLflow port can read every project's traces, so keep it off a
  network shared with people who must not. Do not put sensitive data in traces on a shared alpha
  deployment.
- **Apply has no two-person rule.** One person with the `owner` or `editor` role in the project can
  review and apply a candidate. The approval record is created at Apply time as the audit and rollback
  anchor, and it records who applied. It is not a second approver.
- **CSRF protection is off by default.** `CALIBER_CSRF_ENABLED` defaults to false, on the assumption of a
  loopback or trusted-network deployment. Turn it on, and set a signing secret, before exposing CALIBER
  beyond that.
- **Simulated by default, real with a key.** The library defaults for the LLM and the evaluator are `fake`, and the Docker
  stack's `auto` falls back to them when no `OPENAI_API_KEY` is present, so a prompt or a judge cannot be scored
  (the Evaluations route answers 400 `evaluation requires a real LLM provider`) until a key is configured. The
  provider banner, the Settings page, `/readiness` (`ai_components`, `all_ai_real`) and `./start.sh` say what is
  simulated, and the banner cannot be dismissed while the evaluator or promoter is simulated. An Anthropic key
  alone makes Aria, knowledge-base answers and Claude-model judges real, but not workflow agents or calibration,
  which need OpenAI in this alpha. Aria's planner is rule-based by design; only its chat, drafts and helpers use a model.
- **SQLite needs a separate MLflow store.** CALIBER and MLflow can share one SQLite file in development,
  and startup warns when they do, but only one writer wins at a time. Use PostgreSQL for anything shared.
- **The tool sandbox is a process boundary, not isolation.** Tool code runs in a short-lived,
  environment-empty process with resource limits. Register tools only from authors you trust.
- **Knowledge bases need an S3-compatible bucket**, the `knowledge-local` extra (torch and
  sentence-transformers) and a one-time embedding-model download. Without a reachable object store,
  creating one fails fast with a 503, and without the extra every embedding model is listed as
  unavailable. The default docker image installs `knowledge` but not `knowledge-local`, so it cannot build
  a knowledge base until you add it to `CALIBER_INSTALL_EXTRAS`. The storage and build path is tested
  against a real MinIO and PostgreSQL with simulated embeddings; no CI job exercises a real model.
- **Gate verdicts are not project-scoped.** `/gate-verdicts` keys a verdict by a free-form string that
  names no artifact, so any operator can overwrite any verdict. It is advisory: no release or promotion
  decision reads it.
- **No HA, no performance targets, no SSO or MFA, no multi-tenant hosting.**
- **Backups are documented, not rehearsed.** See [Backup and recovery](m-52-backup-and-recovery.md).
- **No upgrade guarantees** from earlier tags, and the packages are not on PyPI. Build wheels from a
  checkout until the prerelease assets are published.
- **Preview areas may change** or be removed without notice. They are off by default; see [Feature flags](#feature-flags).
